title: No. 40 — On the Powers of the Convention to Form a Mixed Government Examined and Sustained For the New York Packet. Friday, January 18, 1788. (Madison)
paragraphs: The SECOND point to be examined is whether the Convention was authorized to frame and propose this mixed Constitution.

To be exact, we should measure the Convention's powers by examining the commissions that its members received from the bodies that sent them. But every one of those commissions pointed back to one of two recommendations: the one from the meeting at Annapolis in September, 1786, or the one from Congress in February, 1787. So it is enough to look at those two acts.

The act from Annapolis recommends the "appointment of commissioners to take into consideration the situation of the United States; to devise SUCH FURTHER PROVISIONS as shall appear to them necessary to render the Constitution of the federal government ADEQUATE TO THE EXIGENCIES OF THE UNION; and to report such an act for that purpose, to the United States in Congress assembled, as when agreed to by them, and afterwards confirmed by the legislature of every State, will effectually provide for the same."

The act of Congress that made the recommendation reads as follows: "WHEREAS, There is provision in the articles of Confederation and perpetual Union, for making alterations therein, by the assent of a Congress of the United States, and of the legislatures of the several States; and whereas experience hath evinced, that there are defects in the present Confederation; as a mean to remedy which, several of the States, and PARTICULARLY THE STATE OF NEW YORK, by express instructions to their delegates in Congress, have suggested a convention for the purposes expressed in the following resolution; and such convention appearing to be the most probable mean of establishing in these States A FIRM NATIONAL GOVERNMENT:

"Resolved, That in the opinion of Congress it is expedient, that on the second Monday of May next a convention of delegates, who shall have been appointed by the several States, be held at Philadelphia, for the sole and express purpose OF REVISING THE ARTICLES OF CONFEDERATION, and reporting to Congress and the several legislatures such ALTERATIONS AND PROVISIONS THEREIN, as shall, when agreed to in Congress, and confirmed by the States, render the federal Constitution ADEQUATE TO THE EXIGENCIES OF GOVERNMENT AND THE PRESERVATION OF THE UNION."

The authority under which the Convention acted has to be drawn out of these several statements, compared with each other and read fairly. The members were to frame a NATIONAL GOVERNMENT that would be adequate to the EXIGENCIES OF GOVERNMENT, and OF THE UNION. They were also to recast the articles of Confederation in whatever form would accomplish those purposes.

Two rules of interpretation apply here. Plain reason dictates both, and both rest on legal axioms. The first is that each part of an expression should, where possible, be given some meaning and be made to serve a common end. The second is that when the parts cannot be made to fit together, the less important must yield to the more important. The means should be given up for the sake of the end, not the end for the sake of the means.

Now suppose that the expressions defining the Convention's authority really did conflict beyond reconciling. Suppose the Convention judged that no ALTERATIONS and PROVISIONS made in the ARTICLES OF CONFEDERATION could possibly produce a NATIONAL and ADEQUATE GOVERNMENT. Which part of the definition should it have followed, and which should it have set aside? Which part mattered more, and which less? Which was the end, and which the means? Let these questions be answered by the most scrupulous interpreters of delegated powers, and by the most bitter opponents of what the Convention did. Let them say what mattered more to the happiness of the people of America: that the articles of Confederation be set aside, an adequate government be provided and the Union be preserved; or that an adequate government be left out and the articles of Confederation be kept. Let them say whether keeping these articles was the end, with reform of the government as the means of securing it; or whether the end that the articles themselves originally aimed at was a government adequate to the national happiness, to which the articles, being insufficient means, should have been sacrificed.

But must we suppose that these expressions are absolutely irreconcilable? Must we suppose that no ALTERATIONS or PROVISIONS made in the articles of the confederation could possibly shape them into a national and adequate government, the kind of government the Convention has proposed?

Surely no weight will be put on the TITLE here, since changing it could never be taken as using a power that was not granted. ALTERATIONS in the body of the document are expressly authorized, and so are NEW PROVISIONS in it. So the Convention had power to change the title, to add new articles and to alter old ones. Must we then admit that the power was overstepped as long as some of the old articles survive? Anyone who says so should at least draw the line between authorized and usurped innovations. He should show what degree of change falls within ALTERATIONS AND FURTHER PROVISIONS and what degree amounts to a TRANSMUTATION of the government. Will it be said that the alterations should not have touched the substance of the Confederation? The States would never have appointed a convention so solemnly, or described its objects so broadly, if they had not contemplated some SUBSTANTIAL reform. Will it be said that the FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES of the Confederation lay outside the Convention's purview and should not have been changed? I ask, What are these principles? Do they require that the States be treated, in establishing the Constitution, as distinct and independent sovereigns? The proposed Constitution treats them that way. Do they require that the members of the government be appointed by the legislatures and not by the people of the States? One branch of the new government is to be appointed by these legislatures; and under the Confederation the delegates to Congress MAY ALL be appointed directly by the people, and in two States(1) they actually are. Do they require that the government's powers act on the States and not directly on individuals? In some cases, as has been shown, the powers of the new government will act on the States in their collective characters. In some cases, too, the powers of the existing government act directly on individuals. Take cases of capture; of piracy; of the post office; of coins, weights and measures; of trade with the Indians; of claims under grants of land by different States; and above all, of trials by courts-martial in the army and navy, where death may be inflicted without a jury or even a civil magistrate. In all these cases the powers of the Confederation operate directly on the persons and interests of individual citizens. Do these fundamental principles require, in particular, that no tax be levied except through the States as intermediaries? The Confederation itself authorizes a direct tax, to a certain extent, on the post office. Congress has also read the power of coinage as allowing it to draw a tribute directly from that source. But leave these instances aside. Was it not an acknowledged aim of the Convention, and the universal expectation of the people, that the regulation of trade should be placed with the general government in a form that would make it a direct source of general revenue? Had Congress not repeatedly recommended this measure as consistent with the fundamental principles of the Confederation? Had not every State but one, New York herself included, gone far enough along with Congress's plan to accept the PRINCIPLE of the innovation? Finally, do these principles require that the powers of the general government be limited, and that beyond that limit the States keep their sovereignty and independence? We have seen that in the new government, as in the old, the general powers are limited, and that in all cases not listed the States keep their sovereign and independent jurisdiction.

The truth is that the great principles of the Constitution the Convention proposed are better seen as an expansion of principles already found in the articles of Confederation than as something absolutely new. The trouble with the old system is that these principles are so feeble and narrow that they justify every charge of ineffectiveness brought against it, and need to be enlarged so much that the new system looks like a complete transformation of the old.

In one respect it is admitted that the Convention has departed from the terms of its commission. Instead of reporting a plan that needs the confirmation OF THE LEGISLATURES OF ALL THE STATES, it has reported one to be confirmed by the PEOPLE, which can take effect with NINE STATES ONLY. It is worth noting that this objection, though the most plausible, has been pressed the least in the pamphlets and articles that have swarmed out against the Convention. The restraint can only come from an irresistible sense of how absurd it would be to make the fate of twelve States depend on the perverseness or corruption of a thirteenth. It may also come from the example of stubborn opposition given by a MAJORITY of one sixtieth of the people of America to a measure that twelve States, holding fifty-nine sixtieths of the people, had approved and called for. That example is still fresh in the memory, and the indignation, of every citizen who has felt for the wounded honor and prosperity of his country. Since those who have criticized the Convention's powers have more or less dropped this objection, I will set it aside without further comment.
The THIRD point to be examined is how far a sense of duty, arising out of the situation itself, could have made up for any lack of regular authority.

So far we have analyzed and tested the powers of the Convention as strictly, and by the same rules, as if they had been real and final powers to establish a Constitution for the United States. We have seen how they hold up even on that assumption. Now we should remember that the powers were only advisory and recommendatory. The States meant them to be so, and the Convention understood them to be so. The Convention has accordingly planned and proposed a Constitution that will be worth no more than the paper it is written on unless it receives the approval of the people to whom it is addressed. This changes the whole look of the matter, and lets us judge properly the course the Convention took.

Consider the position the Convention was in. We can gather from its proceedings that the members were deeply and unanimously impressed by the crisis, which had led their country, almost with one voice, to try so unusual and solemn an experiment: correcting the errors of the very system that had produced the crisis. They were just as deeply and unanimously convinced that a reform like the one they have proposed was absolutely necessary to accomplish the purposes of their appointment. They could not have been ignorant that the great body of citizens throughout this great empire were waiting with the keenest anxiety for the outcome of their deliberations. They had every reason to believe that the opposite feelings stirred the minds and hearts of every foe, foreign and domestic, of the liberty and prosperity of the United States. They had seen, from the beginning and through the course of the experiment, how readily the PROPOSITION of a single State (Virginia), for a partial amendment of the Confederation, had been taken up and advanced. They had seen the LIBERTY ASSUMED by a VERY FEW deputies from a VERY FEW States, meeting at Annapolis, of recommending a great and critical object that was wholly foreign to their commission, not only justified by public opinion but actually carried out by twelve of the thirteen States. They had seen Congress, many times, take on not only recommendatory but operative powers, and the public approve, on occasions and for objects infinitely less urgent than those that were to govern their own conduct. They must have reflected that in every great change of an established government, forms ought to yield to substance. Rigid adherence to forms in such cases would make the transcendent and precious right of the people to "abolish or alter their governments as to them shall seem most likely to effect their safety and happiness"(2) merely nominal and worthless, since the people cannot move toward their goal spontaneously and all together; and it is therefore essential that such changes be started by some INFORMAL AND UNAUTHORIZED PROPOSITIONS from some patriotic and respectable citizen or group of citizens. They must have recalled that it was through this irregular and self-assumed privilege of proposing to the people plans for their safety and happiness that the States were first united against the danger their ancient government threatened; that committees and congresses were formed to concentrate their efforts and defend their rights; and that CONVENTIONS were ELECTED in THE SEVERAL STATES to establish the constitutions under which they are now governed. Nor could they have forgotten that nobody showed petty, ill-timed scruples or zeal for ordinary forms, except those who wished to hide behind these masks their secret hostility to the substance being fought for. They must have kept in mind that, because the plan they framed and proposed was to be submitted TO THE PEOPLE THEMSELVES, this supreme authority's disapproval would destroy it forever, while its approval would wipe out all earlier errors and irregularities. It might even have occurred to them that, where people are inclined to find fault, neglecting to use the full power vested in them, and still more recommending any measure that their commission did not warrant, would draw as much criticism as recommending, at one stroke, a measure fully equal to the national exigencies.

Suppose the Convention, with all these impressions and in the midst of all these considerations, had not shown a manly confidence in its country, which had singled it out by so particular a confidence, and had not pointed to a system that it judged capable of securing the country's happiness. Suppose it had instead made the cold and sullen decision to disappoint the country's ardent hopes, to sacrifice substance to forms, and to commit the country's dearest interests to the uncertainty of delay and the hazard of events. I would ask any man who can raise his mind to one elevated thought, or stir in his heart one patriotic feeling, what verdict the impartial world, the friends of mankind and every virtuous citizen should have passed on the conduct and character of this assembly. Or if there is a man whose urge to condemn will not be controlled, I would ask what sentence he keeps in reserve for the twelve States that USURPED THE POWER of sending deputies to the Convention, a body wholly unknown to their constitutions; for Congress, which recommended appointing this body, equally unknown to the Confederation; and for the State of New York in particular, which first urged this unauthorized step and then took it.

But to leave the objectors without any pretext, let us grant for a moment that the Convention was neither authorized by its commission nor justified by circumstances in proposing a Constitution to its country. Does it follow that the Constitution must be rejected for that reason alone? According to the noble precept, it is lawful to take good advice even from an enemy. Shall we then set the ignoble example of refusing such advice when our friends offer it? In every case the prudent question is not so much FROM WHOM the advice comes as whether the advice is GOOD.

To sum up what has been argued and proved here: the charge that the Convention exceeded its powers has no foundation, except for one point that the objectors have hardly pressed. Even if the Convention had exceeded its powers, the circumstances it was placed in not only warranted but required it, as the trusted servant of its country, to take the liberty it assumed. And finally, even if it had violated both its powers and its obligations in proposing a Constitution, we should still embrace that Constitution if it is fitted to accomplish the aims and the happiness of the people of America. How far it deserves that description is the subject we are investigating.
1. Connecticut and Rhode Island.
2. Declaration of Independence.
